newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada bonds end firmer after Thiessen, eye on Fed.
newsitem.headline: Canada bonds end firmer after Thiessen, eye on Fed.

text.p: Canadian bonds closed firmer on Friday, helped by comments from Finance Minister Paul Martin and central bank chief Gordon Thiessen, with the market mostly focused on Tuesday's FOMC meeting, analysts said.

"We did see Paul Martin and Thiessen both making very, very upbeat statements about where the economy is going," said Jim Webber, head of fixed-income research with TD Securities Inc. "In the absence of much else to trade on I think that's fairly important."
Canada's 30-year benchmark bond rose C$0.20 to C$108.90 to yield 7.236 percent.
The U.S. 30-year bond fell 1/32 to yield 6.96 percent. The spread between the two narrowed to 28 basis points from 30 basis points at Thursday's close.

In a speech to a group of business economists, Thiessen said there was room for strong growth in output and employment in coming quarters without a resurgence of inflation. Thiessen also said in a press conference that he continues to believe the Canadian dollar is on an upward trend.
Speaking separately, Finance Minister Martin said with the exception of youth unemployment, he was confident the Canadian economy could withstand a hike in U.S. rates next week.

Investors in Canadian bonds largely disregarded a report that Canada's unadjusted February consumer price index rose 0.1 percent in the month and 2.2 percent in the year. Core CPI rose 1.5 percent year-on-year, well within the Bank of Canada's 1.0-3.0 percent target range.
Analysts said the likelihood that the U.S. Federal Reserve will hike rates on Tuesday helped keep bonds in a narrow range, analysts said.
"I don't think anything significant is going to change until we see what Mr Greenspan is going to do next week," said Ted Carmichael, head of research with J.P. Morgan Canada.

In his press conference, Thiessen cautioned against reading a specific course of action into remarks made earlier this week that the Bank of Canada had more room for maneuver in reaction to a possible U.S. rate hike.
In other prices, the Government of Canada's 7.0 percent bond due 2006 rose C$0.11 to C$102.71 to yield 6.615. The U.S. bond fell 4/32 to yield 6.75 percent.
The negative spread between the bonds widened to 14 basis points from 13 basis points on Wednesday.
The three-month cash T-bill yielded 3.18 percent against its U.S. equivalent which yielded 5.40 percent.
